subject: Medicine
summary: Typhoid fever is a systemic infection caused by Salmonella Typhi, transmitted via contaminated food, water, or flies. It presents with prolonged fever, abdominal pain, and rose spots, and can be fatal without prompt treatment.

sections.p: Typhoid fever is a febrile illness caused by Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi. Diagnosis relies on clinical suspicion plus microbiological confirmation.
b: Blood culture positive for S. Typhi (gold standard)
Widal test supportive only in endemic areas

t.b: Does the patient have bacteremia? Positive culture confirms typhoid and guides antibiotics
Is the patient shedding organisms? Positive after the first week indicates carrier state
Are there rising O and H antibodies? May suggest typhoid in endemic settings but has low specificity

sections.p: Severity is graded by complications and response to therapy: uncomplicated, severe (high fever >40 °C, intestinal hemorrhage or perforation), and critical (septic shock).
b: Uncomplicated: fever, malaise, no organ dysfunction

sections.p: The single cause is ingestion of S. Typhi, but risk factors in low‑resource settings increase exposure.
b: Housefly (Musca) transmission from feces to food

sections.p: After 1–2 weeks of incubation, patients develop stepwise fever, headache, abdominal discomfort, and sometimes a maculopapular rose‑spot rash on trunk.
Laboratory work supports diagnosis and monitors complications.

t.b: Low WBC may indicate severe disease; normal WBC does not rule out typhoid
Are transaminases raised? Mild elevation is common; marked rise suggests hepatic involvement or co‑infection
Can we detect S. Typhi later? Useful after first week when bacteremia wanes

sections.p: Complications arise from intestinal ulceration, systemic spread, or immune dysregulation.
Treat the infection with appropriate antibiotics and provide supportive care.
b: First‑line: fluoroquinolones (if susceptibility known) – target DNA gyrase, high intracellular penetration
Alternative: third‑generation cephalosporins – safe in pregnancy, avoid fluoroquinolone resistance
Avoid: chloramphenicol where marrow toxicity is a concern

sections.p: Monitor for relapse, ensure carrier eradication, and vaccinate at‑risk populations.
b: Repeat blood culture after therapy if fever persists
Chronic carrier testing (stool culture) at 3 months
Typhoid conjugate vaccine for endemic areas

sections.p: Other febrile illnesses in the tropics share overlapping features.
Certain tests may be falsely negative or non‑specific.
b: Widal test: high false‑positive rates in endemic areas
Blood culture: may be negative after first week of illness

whenToSeekHelp: Persistent high fever >40 °C despite oral antibiotics
Severe abdominal pain with guarding (possible perforation)
Vomiting blood or passing black stools (GI bleed)

faq.a: Typhoid often shows a lower heart rate than expected for the fever, helping differentiate it from other infections.

faq.q: Can a patient be a chronic carrier?
faq.a: Yes, about 1–5 % become carriers, shedding S. Typhi in stool for months; they need eradication therapy and hygiene counseling.

faq.q: What if blood cultures are unavailable?
faq.a: Use stool culture after the first week or rely on clinical criteria and Widal test cautiously in endemic settings.

exam: Describe the stepwise fever pattern and the significance of relative bradycardia in typhoid.
List the first‑line antibiotic choices for typhoid and explain why fluoroquinolones are preferred when susceptibility is known.
Identify three life‑threatening complications of typhoid and the clinical signs that prompt urgent intervention.
